overview.title: The three-stage text pipeline and a character-level tokenizer
overview.main_topic: Why modern models use only light standardization; the standardization -> splitting -> indexing pipeline (figure 14.1); and Listing 14.1, a CharTokenizer class
overview.central_idea: Heavy standardization such as stemming now tends to hurt large models, because tense and plurality carry meaning, so standardization is kept as light as possible. Text preprocessing has three stages, standardization, splitting and indexing, which together are called tokenization; an object performing them is a tokenizer. Listing 14.1 implements a character-level tokenizer as a class with one method per stage.
overview.importance: It formalizes the preprocessing pipeline that every text model in chapters 14-15 uses, and gives the first reusable tokenizer object, the template for WordTokenizer (p.412) and for Keras-provided tokenizers later.
learning_objectives: Explain why aggressive standardization hurts modern large models
Name and describe the three stages of text preprocessing in figure 14.1
Define tokenization (the whole process) and tokenizer (the object)
Read Listing 14.1 and explain each method of CharTokenizer
Trace figure 14.1's example from "The cat sat on the mat." to token indices
prerequisites: Standardization, splitting and indexing from pp.408-410

summary:
The page finishes the sentence from p.410 about stemming and lemmatization: **as models have grown more expressive, this type of standardization tends to do more harm than good**. The tense and plurality of a word are necessary signals to its meaning. For today's larger models, standardization is as light as possible, for example just converting all inputs to a standard character encoding before further processing.

The authors then summarize the **three distinct stages** of text preprocessing, shown in **figure 14.1**:

1. **Standardization**: normalize input with basic text-to-text transformations;
2. **Splitting**: split the text into sequences of *tokens*;
3. **Indexing**: map the tokens to indices using a *vocabulary*.

Figure 14.1 runs "The cat sat on the mat." through the pipeline: standardized text "the cat sat on the mat", then tokens "the", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "mat", then token indices 3, 26, 65, 9, 3, 133. The repeated "the" gets the same index 3 both times.

People often call the entire process **tokenization**, and an object that maps text to a sequence of token indices a **tokenizer**.

**Section 14.2.1** starts building tokenizers. The first is character-level and maps each character to an integer, using only one standardization step: lowercasing. **Listing 14.1** defines `CharTokenizer`: the constructor stores a vocabulary dict and looks up `unk_id = vocabulary["[UNK]"]`; `standardize` returns `inputs.lower()`; `split` returns `re.findall(r".", inputs)`; `index` maps each token with `self.vocabulary.get(t, self.unk_id)`; and `__call__` chains standardize and split (the final indexing and return lines are on p.412). The vocabulary itself is computed from data in Listing 14.2 on p.412.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Finishing p.410's sentence ("But"), the authors say that as models became more expressive, stemming-style standardization started to do more harm than good, because a word's tense and plurality are necessary signals to its meaning. For today's larger models, standardization is as light as possible, e.g. only converting inputs to a standard character encoding.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Merging "stared" and "staring", or "trophy" and "trophies", throws away information (when something happened, how many there are). A small model with little data might benefit from the pooled statistics, but a large model trained on lots of data can learn these forms itself and needs the information they carry. The safest preprocessing is the most information-preserving one.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why modern tokenizers (including the subword tokenizers of 14.2.2 and the pretrained models of chapter 15) do little more than Unicode normalization, and why the book's own tokenizers only lowercase.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: "a standard character encoding" typically means decoding to Unicode (e.g. UTF-8) and possibly applying Unicode normalization (NFC/NFKC), so visually identical characters share one code-point sequence.

terminology.meaning: A model with enough capacity to learn complex functions, here to learn the relations between word forms from data.
A single consistent representation of characters (such as UTF-8 Unicode) applied to all inputs.

paragraphs.why_it_matters: The same three-stage structure applies at every token granularity; only the split rule and vocabulary change. Keras' TextVectorization layer exposes the same stages as arguments.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The output of indexing is the integer sequence that a model consumes, for example as input to an embedding layer.

concepts.name: Tokenization (three-stage pipeline)
concepts.definition: The entire process of standardization, splitting and indexing that turns text into a sequence of token indices.
concepts.intuition: Clean the text, cut it into pieces, number the pieces.
concepts.technical: standardize: str -> str; split: str -> list[str]; index: list[str] -> list[int] using a vocabulary with an [UNK] fallback.
concepts.significance: Every text model in the book consumes the output of such a pipeline.
concepts.example: "The cat sat on the mat." -> "the cat sat on the mat" -> [the, cat, sat, on, the, mat] -> [3, 26, 65, 9, 3, 133] (figure 14.1).
concepts.misconception: Tokenization is not only splitting; the book uses the word for the whole pipeline.

concepts.name: Tokenizer
concepts.definition: An object that maps text to a sequence of token indices.
concepts.intuition: A function object holding a vocabulary and the rules for using it.
concepts.technical: In Listing 14.1, a Python class with standardize, split and index methods; __call__ runs them in order, so tokenizer(text) returns indices.
concepts.significance: It bundles the preprocessing so the same rules apply to training and test data.
concepts.example: char_tokenizer = CharTokenizer(vocabulary); char_tokenizer("Hi") -> indices of "h" and "i".
concepts.misconception: A tokenizer needs a vocabulary built beforehand; Listing 14.1 takes it as a constructor argument and does not build it.

concepts.name: Light standardization for large models
concepts.definition: Keeping standardization minimal (e.g. a standard character encoding) because tense and plurality are necessary signals to meaning.
concepts.intuition: Don't throw away information that a big model could use.
concepts.technical: Stemming/lemmatization merge inflections; this reduces vocabulary but loses grammatical information. Expressive models learn the relations between word forms themselves.
concepts.significance: Explains modern practice and why the book's tokenizers only lowercase.
concepts.example: "stared" vs. "staring": tense matters for meaning, so don't merge them.
concepts.misconception: Standardization is not all-or-nothing; even modern pipelines normalize the encoding.

code.title: A basic character-level tokenizer (continues on p.412)
code.what_it_does: Defines a class implementing the three-stage pipeline for characters. This page shows the class up to tokens = self.split(inputs); the remaining two lines of __call__ (indices = self.index(tokens) and return indices) are on p.412.

line_explanations.explanation: The constructor stores a token -> index dict and caches the index of [UNK] as unk_id, so the fallback is not hard-coded as 0 (unlike p.410). It raises KeyError if the vocabulary lacks [UNK].
Splitting: the "." regex from p.408 gives one token per character.
Indexing: look up each token, falling back to unk_id.
__call__ makes the instance callable: standardize, then split (continued on p.412 with indexing and return).

code.inputs_outputs: Construct with a vocabulary dict containing "[UNK]". Calling with a string returns a list of ints, one per character (completed on p.412).
code.algorithm: lower() -> findall(".") -> dict lookup with default.
code.theory_link: A direct implementation of figure 14.1's standardize/split/index stages at character granularity.

parameters.name: vocabulary
parameters.role: Dict mapping characters (and "[UNK]") to indices; built by compute_char_vocabulary (Listing 14.2, p.412).

parameters.name: unk_id
parameters.role: Index for characters not in the vocabulary.

pitfalls: The regex "." skips newlines, so line breaks are not tokenized (relevant when lines come from a file, as on p.413).
Relies on re (the regex package) having been imported earlier (p.408).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written illustration (not from the book), assuming the full class from pp.411-412
vocab = {"[UNK]": 0, " ": 1, "t": 2, "h": 3, "e": 4, "a": 5}
tok = CharTokenizer(vocab)
print(tok("The hat"))   # ['t','h','e',' ','h','a','t'] -> [2, 3, 4, 1, 3, 5, 2]
print(tok("Thy"))       # 'y' unknown -> [2, 3, 0]

deeper.title: Following figure 14.1 stage by stage
deeper.body:
1. **Text**: `The cat sat on the mat.`
2. **Standardized text**: `the cat sat on the mat` (lowercased, period removed).
3. **Tokens**: `"the", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "mat"` (word-level split).
4. **Token indices**: `3, 26, 65, 9, 3, 133`.

The two occurrences of "the" both map to 3, which shows that indexing is a deterministic lookup, not a position. The specific numbers come from some vocabulary not shown in the figure, so they are illustrative.

deeper.title: Why the pipeline is split into methods
deeper.body: Splitting the tokenizer into `standardize`, `split` and `index` makes each stage replaceable. Listing 14.3 (p.412) builds the word tokenizer by changing only `split`'s regex. A subclass could also add accent removal to `standardize` without touching the rest. This mirrors how library tokenizers expose standardization and splitting as configurable options.

deeper.title: Why stemming hurts: an example
deeper.body: Consider sentiment: "The plot *was* good" vs. "The plot *is* good... until the end." Or count-sensitive tasks: "one trophy" vs. "many trophies". A stemmer maps "trophies" -> "trophy" and "stared"/"staring" -> "stare", erasing distinctions a large model could use. With millions of examples, the model sees enough of every form to learn their relation, so merging buys nothing and costs information. (Illustrative examples, not from the book.)

misconceptions.claim: Modern NLP still relies on stemming and heavy normalization.
misconceptions.correction: For the larger models used today, most standardization is as light as possible, because tense and plurality are necessary signals to meaning.

misconceptions.claim: "Tokenization" means only splitting text into tokens.
misconceptions.correction: The book notes that people often use it for the entire process (standardize, split, index); an object doing all of it is a tokenizer.

misconceptions.claim: Token indices in figure 14.1 encode word positions.
misconceptions.correction: They are vocabulary lookups: "the" maps to 3 in both positions.

takeaways: Stemming-style standardization tends to do more harm than good for expressive modern models; tense and plurality carry meaning.
For large models, standardization is as light as possible, e.g. a standard character encoding.
Text preprocessing has three stages: standardization, splitting, indexing (figure 14.1).
The whole process is often called tokenization; the object doing it is a tokenizer.
Listing 14.1's CharTokenizer has one method per stage: lower(), findall("."), and a vocabulary lookup with unk_id.
The vocabulary is passed in; computing it from data comes in Listing 14.2.

questions.question: Why does heavy standardization like stemming tend to hurt today's larger models?
options: It makes the vocabulary too large
Tense and plurality are necessary signals to a word's meaning and get erased
It cannot be implemented with regular expressions
Large models cannot process lowercase text
questions.answer: Tense and plurality are necessary signals to a word's meaning and get erased
questions.explanation: The book says exactly this. Stemming shrinks the vocabulary rather than enlarging it, it was historically done with regexes, and lowercase text is no problem for any model.

questions.question: List the three stages of text preprocessing in order and what each produces.
questions.answer: Standardization (normalized text), splitting (a sequence of tokens), indexing (a sequence of integer indices via a vocabulary).
questions.explanation: This is the numbered list and figure 14.1.

questions.question: In figure 14.1, why does "the" map to 3 in both positions?
questions.answer: Indexing is a vocabulary lookup that depends only on the token string, not its position, so the same token always gets the same index.
questions.explanation: The vocabulary maps each distinct token to one index.

questions.question: In CharTokenizer, what happens when index() meets a character not in the vocabulary?
options: It returns self.unk_id for that character
It adds the character to the vocabulary
questions.answer: It returns self.unk_id for that character
questions.explanation: index uses self.vocabulary.get(t, self.unk_id). A KeyError could only occur in __init__ if [UNK] were missing; nothing is skipped and the vocabulary is never modified.

questions.question: What is the only standardization step CharTokenizer applies?
questions.explanation: "To keep things simple, we will use only one standardization step—we lowercase all input."

questions.question: What is the purpose of defining __call__ in CharTokenizer?
questions.answer: It makes the tokenizer instance callable like a function, so tokenizer(text) runs standardize -> split -> index and returns indices.
questions.explanation: __call__ chains the stage methods; the final index and return lines are on p.412.

questions.question: Can you explain, without notes, the difference between the narrow and the broad meaning of "tokenization"?
questions.answer: Narrow: only the splitting step. Broad (as the book uses it here): the entire standardize-split-index process.
questions.explanation: See the paragraph "People often refer to the entire process as tokenization...".
